odd.e: From Middle English odde, od (“odd (not even); leftover after division into pairs”), from Old Norse oddi (“odd, third or additional number; triangle”), from oddr (“point of a weapon”), from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“point”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to stick, prick, pierce, sting”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to set, place”).
odd.g: Differing from what is usual, ordinary or expected.

odious.e: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).
odious.g: Arousing or meriting strong dislike, aversion, or intense displeasure.

odor.e: From Middle English odour, borrowed from Anglo-Norman odour, from Old French odor, from Latin odor.
odor.g: Any smell, whether fragrant or offensive.
